clue.text: Numerically speaking, the catch of this particular puzzle

definitions.text: Numerically speaking, the catch of this particular puzzle

parts.words: Numerically speaking, the catch of this particular puzzle
parts.note: this puzzle is No 12,345, and the counting rhyme 'One, two, three, four, five' goes on to say what was caught

explanation.surface: A setter asks what this puzzle's prize catch is, in numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle number 12345 is the opening of the nursery counting rhyme 'One, two, three, four, five, once I caught a fish alive', so the 'catch' of puzzle 12345 is what the rhyme says was caught.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyme that counts one to five names a live fish as the thing caught, matching the puzzle's number.

clue.text: Though hearts may be sweet, diamonds are the best for a girl

definitions.text: Though hearts may be sweet, diamonds are the best for a girl

parts.words: Though hearts may be sweet, diamonds are the best for a girl
parts.note: plays on the song title 'Diamonds Are a Girl's Best ...', with sweethearts set against jewels

explanation.surface: Romance is nice, but a girl would rather have jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: The song line 'Diamonds are a girl's best friend' supplies the missing word; 'sweet hearts' hints at sweethearts, the rival kind of companion.
explanation.definitionFit: The well-known song says diamonds are a girl's best companion, so the word that completes it is the answer.

clue.text: Put down iron after. Bob gets up

indicators.note: after says the iron piece comes behind the shilling-and-up pieces

parts.note: a bob was slang for a shilling, abbreviated s in old British money
taken as written
to iron clothes is to press them

explanation.surface: Someone sets the iron down once Bob has got out of bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' looks like a man's name but is old British slang for a shilling, whose abbreviation was s; 'gets' is only a link, and 'after' sets the iron last.
explanation.definitionFit: To suppress a revolt is to crush or quell it, the same as putting it down.

clue.text: South Scotland, might one say?

parts.note: reads 'Scotland' as Scott's land, the polar territory linked with Captain Scott's expedition to the South Pole

explanation.surface: A question about the southern part of Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Scotland here is not the country: split it as Scot(t)-land, the land of Captain Robert Scott, who died returning from the South Pole in 1912.
explanation.definitionFit: The continent round the South Pole is where Captain Scott made his famous expedition, so it could be called his land.

clue.text: Eli's inglorious grandson

parts.note: in the Book of Samuel the priest Eli's grandson is given a name meaning 'the glory has departed'

explanation.surface: A biblical priest's grandson with no glory to his name.
explanation.walkthrough: In 1 Samuel 4 the child born as the Ark is captured is named for the departed glory of Israel; 'inglorious' translates his name.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical name means 'no glory', and its bearer was the grandson of the priest Eli.

clue.text: Stage direction superfluous with a bear in pursuit?

definitions.text: Stage direction superfluous with a bear in pursuit?

parts.words: Stage direction superfluous with a bear in pursuit?
parts.note: an actor chased by a bear needs no telling to leave

explanation.surface: Why give an actor directions when a bear is chasing him?
explanation.walkthrough: The Winter's Tale has the famous direction 'Exit, pursued by a bear'; the clue asks whether the order to leave is needed when a bear is already chasing.
explanation.definitionFit: The script word telling an actor to leave the stage is the one used in Shakespeare's bear direction.

clue.text: Wherewith, in lists of graduates, one squares accounts?

parts.note: BA, Bachelor of Arts, stands for graduates
the lists were jousting arenas, so lances are the weapons found in lists

explanation.surface: Asks how one settles up, among lists of university graduates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lists' are not registers but the tilting grounds of medieval jousting, where knights carried lances; BA is the graduate's degree.
explanation.definitionFit: A bookkeeper who balances accounts makes the two sides equal, which is to square them.

clue.text: Where modern exploration scores is not the bullring

definitions.text: Where modern exploration scores is not the bullring

parts.words: Where modern exploration scores is not the bullring
parts.note: on an archery or darts target the scoring ring round the bull is the outer, and modern explorers travel beyond Earth

explanation.surface: Modern explorers don't score their successes in a bullfighting arena.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bullring' suggests bullfighting, but it is the bull of a target: a hit outside it lands in the outer, while 'modern exploration' points to rockets beyond the atmosphere.
explanation.definitionFit: Astronauts explore the region beyond Earth's atmosphere, and on a target the zone beyond the bull is the outer.

clue.text: A person from Porlock broke in upon this scene

definitions.text: A person from Porlock broke in upon this scene

parts.words: A person from Porlock broke in upon this scene
parts.note: Coleridge said a visitor from Porlock interrupted him while writing his dream poem Kubla Khan

explanation.surface: A visitor from a Somerset village interrupted someone's view.
explanation.walkthrough: Coleridge claimed 'a person on business from Porlock' broke his dream as he wrote Kubla Khan, which opens 'In Xanadu did Kubla Khan'.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem left unfinished after the Porlock visitor is set in Kubla Khan's summer capital.

clue.text: Send a message

explanation.surface: An instruction to send off a note.
explanation.definitionFit: To dispatch is to send off, and a dispatch is also a written report or communique.

clue.text: After the fourth act make tea and start working

indicators.note: after says the rearranged tea comes behind the fourth act

parts.note: taken as written
IV is four in Roman numerals, so the fourth act is act IV

indicators.note: to make something of tea is to rework its letters into a new order

explanation.surface: A play's interval: once act four ends, brew a pot and get going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make tea' sounds domestic but is the anagram signal on the drink's own letters, and 'After' places them behind the Roman-numbered act.
explanation.definitionFit: To activate a machine is to set it going or bring it into operation.

clue.text: Tool for tots, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the word for totting is sounded, not spelt

parts.note: to tot up a column of figures is to add it, so tots means adds

explanation.surface: A tool made for small children, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tots' looks like small children but is the verb: tots up means adds; 'for' only links the tool to it.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a carpenter's cutting tool, like an axe with its blade set crosswise.

clue.text: Case for the prosecution

parts.note: a grammatical case named from the Latin for accusing, as if belonging to the prosecuting side in court

explanation.surface: The evidence a prosecutor brings to court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' is not the legal argument but a grammatical case: the one whose name means 'accusing' suits the prosecution.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin grammatical case for direct objects takes its name from accusing, the prosecutor's role.

clue.text: Four-or single-handed accompaniment in a Chinese restaurant?

definitions.text: Four-or single-handed accompaniment in a Chinese restaurant?

parts.words: Four-or single-handed accompaniment in a Chinese restaurant?
parts.note: a simple piano tune played solo or as a duet shares its name with the eating sticks of a Chinese meal

explanation.surface: Musical entertainment offered with dinner at a Chinese restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'accompaniment' sounds musical, and the beginner's piano waltz of this name can be played by one or two players, but at the table it is the pair of eating sticks.
explanation.definitionFit: The utensils used for eating in Chinese restaurants share their name with a well-known simple piano waltz.

clue.text: Where the race begins on the Devon coast

definitions.text: Where the race begins on the Devon coast

parts.words: Where the race begins on the Devon coast
parts.note: a headland in south Devon shares its name with the line where a race begins

explanation.surface: Asks where a coastal race in Devon gets under way.
explanation.walkthrough: Devon is a county in south-west England; the headland near Dartmouth bears the same name as a race's opening mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A race begins at its opening mark, and a promontory on the south Devon coast carries that same name.

clue.text: "Thy hyacinth hair, thy face " (Poe)

parts.note: a quotation from Poe's poem To Helen with one word left blank for the solver to fill

explanation.surface: A line from Edgar Allan Poe with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Poe's 'To Helen' reads 'Thy hyacinth hair, thy classic face'; the gap takes the missing adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective Poe used describes Helen's face as having the timeless beauty of ancient Greece.

clue.text: Exemplified by the force of the Hurricane

definitions.text: Exemplified by the force of the Hurricane

parts.words: Exemplified by the force of the Hurricane
parts.note: the Hurricane was a wartime RAF fighter plane, so its might is military strength in the sky

explanation.surface: Describes the destructive force of a great storm.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hurricane is not a storm but the Hawker Hurricane, the RAF fighter of the Battle of Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Military strength in the skies, shown by fighter planes such as the Hurricane.

clue.text: It's sort of rummy as an act, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints the letters of the phrase may be one arrangement of something else

explanation.surface: Something strange put on as a performance, maybe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rummy' reads as 'odd', but it is the card game family; the anagram signal is 'perhaps' on AS AN ACT.
explanation.definitionFit: This card game played with two packs is a member of the rummy family.

clue.text: Being forward the trainer is worried about nothing

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go round the zero
worried suggests the trainer's letters are agitated into a new order

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A coach frets over nothing while being pushy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worried' makes ANTERIR from TRAINER, and 'about' puts it round O for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: In anatomy, the front-facing part is described with this word, meaning situated towards the front.

clue.text: A tricky subtlety

parts.note: in bridge, a play to win a trick with a lower card is a skilful subtle move, so tricky means to do with tricks

explanation.surface: A clever, devious refinement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tricky' reads as cunning, but it also points to bridge tricks: the skilful card play of this name tries to win one.
explanation.definitionFit: Delicate skill or subtlety, and in bridge a manoeuvre to take a trick with a lower card.

clue.text: Country backs no visionary type of artist

indicators.note: backs says the country abbreviation is read in the reverse direction

parts.note: RUS is the abbreviation for Russia
a practical person who is no dreamer is a realist

explanation.surface: A nation supports an artist who lacks vision.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backs' looks like 'supports' but is the reversal signal on the Russian abbreviation; the hard-headed non-dreamer is the opposite of the dream painters the answer names.
explanation.definitionFit: Dali and Magritte belonged to this movement of painters depicting dream imagery.

clue.text: Does this fish drink like one?

explanation.surface: Does this fish drink like a fish?
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's 'like one' points to the phrase 'drink like a fish'; the small shark of that name shares its spelling with an old verb for drinking heavily.
explanation.definitionFit: A small shark of European waters, and an old verb meaning to booze habitually.

clue.text: An apt end to one more learned than wise

indicators.note: to here means turned into, so the letters of the apt ending are made into something new

explanation.surface: A fitting finish for a scholar who knows much but understands little.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal is slight: APT END turned 'to' a new order gives the answer, and 'An' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who parades book learning over good sense is a classic fusspot scholar.

clue.text: A bit of brass calling for push and pull!

definitions.text: A bit of brass calling for push and pull!

parts.words: A bit of brass calling for push and pull!
parts.note: a brass instrument whose slide is pushed and pulled to change the note; calling also suggests a job needing influence

explanation.surface: A job in management needing pushiness and connections.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brass' suggests top management and 'push and pull' influence, but this brass instrument is played by working a slide in and out.
explanation.definitionFit: This slide instrument in the brass section is played by pushing and pulling the slide.

clue.text: The monster is therefore upset

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means the word is turned upwards, read from bottom to top

parts.note: ergo is Latin for therefore

explanation.surface: The monster is therefore distressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' reads as distressed, but in a down clue it turns ERGO up the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A man-eating giant of fairy tales is a classic monster.

clue.text: Oriental brand

parts.note: brand is a poetic word for a sword, so an eastern sword with a curved blade

explanation.surface: A trade name from the East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brand' is not a trade name but the old poetic word for a sword.
explanation.definitionFit: A curved single-edged sword from the Middle East is an eastern blade.

clue.text: His prospects are more colourful than ever

definitions.text: His prospects are more colourful than ever

parts.words: His prospects are more colourful than ever
parts.note: prospects read as scenes looked at, which for someone watching colour television are brighter than before

explanation.surface: Someone's future looks brighter than it ever has.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prospects' sounds like future chances, but here they are views: the scenes someone looks at.
explanation.definitionFit: A person watching is an onlooker, whose prospects are literally the views seen.

clue.text: To whom politicians choose to make speeches

definitions.text: To whom politicians choose to make speeches

parts.note: to choose by vote is to elect
to make speeches is to orate

explanation.surface: Politicians decide to address the voters.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines and builds: ELECT for 'choose' and ORATE for 'make speeches' are the two things voters and politicians do.
explanation.definitionFit: Politicians address their speeches to the body of voters who choose them.
